title: Causes of miscarriage | NHS inform
text:
Causes of miscarriage
If you’ve had a miscarriage, it’s natural to want to know why it happened. Most of the time there’s no clear explanation for why you had a miscarriage. It’s unlikely that your miscarriage was caused by anything you did or did not do. This means there’s nothing that could have prevented it.
There are illnesses and conditions that can sometimes cause a miscarriage.
There are also conditions that increase the risk of miscarriage. These conditions are not the reason a miscarriage happens. But, having them means you’re more likely to have a miscarriage.
Age of either parent
The older either parent is, the higher the risk of miscarriage. This is because:
the number and quality of eggs gets lower as someone gets older
the chance of chromosomal abnormalities in sperm increases as someone ages
If you’re carrying a baby, the risk of miscarriage is:
1 in 5 by age 30
1 in 2 by age 40
Blood clotting problems
Blood clotting problems are conditions that make your blood more likely to clot. These conditions include
antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)
,
systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
and thrombophilia.
Babies get the nutrients and oxygen they need from their mother’s blood. The blood flows from your placenta (an organ in your uterus) to your baby’s umbilical cord. If you have a blood clotting disorder, it can reduce the amount of blood going to your placenta. This then causes the blood in the placenta to clot, stopping it from functioning properly.
If this happens, your baby will be unable to get the oxygen and nutrition it needs. This can cause a miscarriage.
Blood clotting disorders can cause both
early
and
late miscarriages
. They can also be a cause of
recurrent miscarriages
.
If you have a blood clotting problem, a doctor, nurse or midwife can discuss treatment options with you.
Cervical insufficiency (weak cervix)
The cervix is the entrance to your uterus (womb). Some people have a weak or damaged cervix. In these cases, it can open too soon in your pregnancy. This can be a cause of a
late miscarriage
and premature birth.
If you’re at increased risk for cervical insufficiency, you’ll be offered screening for problems. This will be done by an ultrasound scan. If cervical insufficiency is suspected, medical professionals will discuss your treatment options with you.
Read more about cervical insufficiency
Chromosome conditions
Your baby inherits genetic material called chromosomes from both of their parents. Sometimes the chromosomes a parent passes on are abnormal. This can happen even if both parents have normal chromosomes.
If your baby inherits a chromosome condition, they’ll not be able to develop properly. This causes a miscarriage.
It’s not possible to tell which parent passed on the chromosome condition.
Chromosome conditions are thought to be the most common cause of an
early miscarriage
.
Developmental problems with your baby
Some babies do not develop as expected. This can cause changes in their anatomy (body). If your baby has not developed as expected, this can cause a
late miscarriage
.
Ethnicity
Evidence suggests that black and black mixed heritage women have a higher rate of miscarriage.
Read more about the risk of miscarriage for black and black mixed heritage women
Fibroids
Fibroids are growths of muscle and tissue in the wall of the uterus. These growths are different for every person who has them. They may increase the risk of a miscarriage, but it depends on their size and position. Not all fibroids increase the risk of miscarriage.
Food poisoning
Food poisoning increases the risk of both
early
and
late miscarriage
.
Food poisoning is caused by eating food that contains bacteria, viruses or parasites. These can make you very ill, which increases the risk of miscarriage.
To reduce the risk of getting food poisoning, you should:
follow the current advice about what you can safely eat and drink during pregnancy
store and chill food correctly, following recommended guidance
prepare and cook food carefully, following food hygiene rules
Even if you do get food poisoning, it does not mean you’ll have a miscarriage.
Hormonal imbalances
The risk of early or late miscarriage increases if you have too many or not enough of certain hormones.
Conditions that cause hormonal imbalances within the body include:
problems with your thyroid gland
diabetes
problems with your pituitary gland
Infection
Some types of infection can cause both
early
and
late miscarriages
. These infections include:
parvovirus
cytomegalovirus (CMV)
listeria
toxoplasmosis
Lifestyle factors
Some lifestyle factors have been shown to increase the risk of miscarriage. These include:
smoking or using tobacco products
being above or below a healthy weight
drinking alcohol or using illegal drugs during pregnancy
consuming over 200mcg of caffeine a day (around 2 mugs of instant coffee)
It’s important to remember that these factors increase the risk of miscarriage. They do not cause miscarriage. If you consumed a little alcohol before discovering you were pregnant, it’s very unlikely to have caused a miscarriage. But, changing these lifestyle factors for the better will reduce your risk of miscarriage in the future.
Read more about stopping smoking
Read more about diet and nutrition
Get support to reduce the amount of alcohol you drink
Get support to help you stop using illegal drugs
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
is a hormone imbalance. It causes problems with your ovaries, and can make getting pregnant difficult. Having PCOS also slightly increases the risk of miscarriage.
Read more about polycystic ovary syndrome
Previous miscarriages
If you’ve had 3 or more miscarriages, you’re at a higher risk of having another. This includes any miscarriages you had before a successful pregnancy. The 3 miscarriages do not need to have happened one after the other.
If you’ve had 3 or more miscarriages, this is called
recurrent miscarriage
.
Problems with the placenta
If there’s a problem with your placenta, it can lead to miscarriage or stillbirth.
Problems with the placenta can cause both
early
and
late miscarriages
.
You’ll be offered an ultrasound scan at 20 weeks which will look at your placenta. If medical professionals identify that you’re at risk of having problems with your placenta, they’ll assess how well blood is flowing to your womb. They’ll also discuss your options with you.
Uterus shape
An unusually shaped uterus increases the risk of both
early
and
late miscarriages
.
The uterus (womb) is the organ where your baby grows when it’s developing. If you have an unusually shaped uterus, you’re more likely to have a miscarriage.
To increase the risk of miscarriage, your uterus needs to be very unusually shaped. A small abnormality does not appear to increase the risk of miscarriage.
Read more about uterine abnormality
